issues.legal_issue: A prior prosecution for commencing construction without permission does not bar a later proceeding seeking demolition for independent breaches of building rules.
material_facts: The earlier prosecution charged the owner only with commencing construction without written permission, and resulted in a fine.
The later demolition application relied on breaches of building rules that were independent of the charge in the earlier prosecution.
The statute expressly made proceedings under a different offence provision mutually exclusive with demolition proceedings, but the Corporation had not proceeded under that offence provision.
issues.conclusion: The earlier prosecution did not preclude the Corporation from instituting the demolition proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The provisos to sections 363 and 493 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923 made proceedings under those sections mutually exclusive, but did not extend that bar to a prosecution under section 488 read with Rule 62 of Schedule XVII. Where the Legislature provides proceedings under different sections for the same facts with different penalties, the proceedings are distinct; absent a bar under section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, proceedings under one section are not treated as proceedings under the other. The statute also contained no bar based on constructive res judicata or on the Corporation's failure to seek demolition in the earlier proceeding.

predicates.demolition_application: A public authority applied for an order requiring the removal of construction that allegedly breached building requirements.
predicates.prior_prosecution_for_distinct_offence: The person responsible for the construction was previously prosecuted for a distinct offence arising from the construction.
predicates.prior_charge_only_unauthorized_commencem: The earlier prosecution charged only that construction had begun without required permission.
predicates.later_application_based_on_independent_b: The later application relied on building-rule breaches independent of the earlier charge.

issues.definition: When a demolition application relies on independent building-rule breaches after a prosecution charging only unauthorized commencement, the earlier prosecution does not bar the demolition application.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution charged solely as commencing construction without permission does not provide a basis for ordering demolition in that prosecution when the offence is complete upon commencement.
material_facts: The earlier complaint charged the owner solely with constructing without permission under Rule 62 of Schedule XVII.
That rule's prohibition was breached when construction commenced, regardless of whether construction was later continued or completed.
The later demolition application concerned breaches of other building rules.
issues.conclusion: No demolition order could have been made under section 536 in the earlier prosecution because the charge was based solely on breach of Rule 62.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 536 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, the possibility of directing demolition depended on the ground on which the prosecution was founded. A charge of commencing construction without permission was complete upon commencement and did not itself raise a question of demolition. Demolition could arise where construction was carried on or completed contrary to permission or in breach of the Act or rules.

predicates.prosecution_for_unauthorized_constructio: A person was prosecuted in connection with construction alleged to have been carried out unlawfully.
predicates.charge_only_concerns_commencement_withou: The prosecution charged only that construction began without required permission.

issues.definition: In a prosecution charging only commencement of construction without permission, the charge does not permit a demolition order in that prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: The authority deciding a demolition application has discretion whether to order demolition when building requirements have been breached.
material_facts: The application sought demolition of construction alleged to have been erected without permission and in breach of building rules.
The courts below treated the decision whether to order demolition as discretionary.
The relevant statutory provision used the word “may,” and an earlier decision had construed materially identical language as conferring discretion.
issues.conclusion: The word “may” confers discretion; demolition is not required as a matter of course whenever a building requirement has been breached.
issues.legal_principle: Section 363 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923 gives the Magistrate discretion whether to order demolition. The Court relied on Abdul Samad v. Corporation of Calcutta, which construed materially identical language in section 449 of the earlier Calcutta Municipal Act as discretionary, and reasoned that the Legislature's reenactment of the language reflected acceptance of that construction.

predicates.demolition_application: A public authority applied for an order requiring the removal of construction that allegedly breached building requirements.
predicates.building_requirement_breached: The construction was shown to have been carried out without required permission, contrary to permission, or in breach of applicable building requirements.

issues.definition: When building requirements have been breached in a demolition proceeding, the decision-maker may choose whether to order demolition.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court generally may not interfere with a discretionary demolition decision unless it rests on a factual mistake or a misunderstanding of the applicable principles.
material_facts: The Magistrate and the High Court declined demolition based on asserted delay, the earlier fine, and the absence of neighbour complaints.
The proceedings for demolition had begun before the earlier fine was imposed, and the delay in the proceedings was not shown to be attributable to the Corporation.
The earlier prosecution and the demolition application concerned different defaults, and the absence of a public complaint did not determine whether the public interest had been harmed.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts' discretionary decisions could not be upheld because they rested on mistakes and misdirections about the timing, the relationship between the charges, and the relevance of the asserted grounds.
issues.legal_principle: A discretionary order is generally not liable to appellate interference unless it is based on a mistake of fact or a misapprehension of the applicable principles. The Court held that the asserted delay was incorrectly assessed, that the earlier fine did not establish punishment twice for the same default, and that the absence of neighbour complaints was not by itself material to whether demolition was appropriate.

predicates.appeal_reviewing_discretionary_demolitio: An appellate court is reviewing a decision whether to order demolition.
predicates.decision_based_on_factual_mistake: The decision rests on a factually mistaken understanding of what occurred or when it occurred.
predicates.decision_based_on_misunderstood_principl: The decision rests on an incorrect understanding of the principles governing the demolition decision.

issues.definition: An appellate court may interfere with a discretionary demolition decision when it rests on a factual mistake or a misunderstanding of the governing principles.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of complaints from neighbours does not by itself determine whether demolition is warranted, although a complaint may be evidence of harm to the public interest.
material_facts: The lower courts relied in part on the absence of complaints from residents near the construction.
The building rules were enacted generally for the benefit of the public.
The relevant assessment was whether the breaches were trivial or serious and likely to adversely affect the public interest.
issues.conclusion: The absence of neighbour complaints was not by itself material to the demolition decision, although a complaint could be evidence of adverse effects on the public interest.
issues.legal_principle: In a proceeding seeking demolition for breach of building rules, the decision-maker must consider whether the breach is formal or trivial, such that a fine may suffice, or serious and likely to affect the public interest adversely. The absence of a complaint is not independently material, though an actual complaint may be evidence of public harm.

predicates.demolition_application: A public authority applied for an order requiring the removal of construction that allegedly breached building requirements.
predicates.building_rule_breach: The construction was carried out in breach of an applicable building rule.
predicates.absence_of_neighbour_complaint: No neighbour or local resident complained about the construction.

issues.definition: In a demolition proceeding involving a building-rule breach, the absence of neighbour complaints does not independently decide whether demolition is warranted.

issues.legal_issue: Demolition may be declined in a particular appeal despite serious building-rule breaches and errors in the decisions below when the passage of time and the public interest do not warrant demolition.
material_facts: The Court found that the owner's conduct in completing the construction in defiance of the law and the serious breaches could justify demolition.
Nearly five years had passed since the building was completed, although the demolition proceeding had been instituted in time.
The Court concluded that the public interest did not call for demolition after that passage of time.
The appeal had come before the Court on a certificate to obtain decisions on important questions, and that purpose had been achieved.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to order demolition and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Although section 363(2) restricted the institution of a demolition application after five years, that limit did not bar an application instituted in time. The Court nevertheless considered the passage of nearly five years, the absence of a present public interest requiring demolition, and the purpose for which the certified appeal had been brought, and concluded that demolition should not be ordered in the circumstances.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_demolition_dec: The Supreme Court is hearing an appeal from a decision on whether construction should be demolished.
predicates.proceeding_instituted_in_time: The demolition proceeding was instituted within the applicable period for commencing it.
predicates.building_completed_nearly_five_years_ear: Nearly five years had passed since the construction was completed.
predicates.public_interest_does_not_require_demolit: The Court concluded that the public interest did not require demolition at that stage.
predicates.appeal_seeks_resolution_of_important_que: The appeal was brought to obtain a decision on important legal questions.

issues.definition: When a timely demolition proceeding reaches the Supreme Court after nearly five years, the public interest does not require demolition, and the appeal seeks resolution of important questions, demolition may be declined.
